text.en: A torch lights when we press the switch and goes off when we release it. Behind that is a complete path for electricity called a circuit.

An electric cell supplies energy to a circuit. Joining cells can make a battery. In everyday speech, we also call some single cells batteries. A simple lamp circuit needs an energy source, conducting connections and a lamp. A switch is useful because it lets us open and close the path. Electricity flows only if the circuit is closed, a complete loop. An open circuit has a gap, so no current flows.
Circuit diagrams use symbols. For a cell, the longer line is positive and the shorter line is negative. A common lamp symbol is a circle with a cross.
Copper, iron and aluminium allow electric current to pass readily. The plastic coatings used on suitable wires are poor conductors. They are examples of insulators. Wires have a metal core and a plastic cover for safety.
In a series circuit the bulbs are joined one after another. If one bulb fuses, all go off. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own path. If one fuses, the others stay on. House wiring is parallel.
Never touch electric wires or switches with wet hands, and never put anything in sockets. Use only cells for experiments, never the mains.

Imagine opening a teacher’s model torch. Start at a cell, follow a connection to the lamp and trace the connection back to the other end of the cell.
Find the two terminals on a cell in the diagram. The raised end of a typical cylindrical torch cell is positive and the flat end is negative. Look for the signs on its casing.

board.text: Find the positive and negative signs

text.en: In a holder with two cells, trace how one cell contacts its neighbour. A cell’s orientation matters. Reversing a cell can change how the cells work together.

board.text: Match the holder’s plus and minus markings

text.en: Look closely at an incandescent torch lamp. The fine wire inside is called its filament. A current through it makes it hot enough to glow.
The lamp has two electrical contacts. In a typical torch bulb, one contact is the small metal tip on the bottom and the other is the metal case near the base.
Another torch may use a light-emitting diode, called an LED. In a simple direct-current circuit, it needs to be connected in the correct direction and used with the right circuit parts.
A supervised classroom kit can include an LED ready to connect safely. If the lamp does not light, follow the kit markings and ask the teacher to check the connections.

board.text: Use a teacher-provided kit and marked connections

text.en: Compare a switch drawn open with one drawn closed. The open switch shows a separation at the contacts. The closed switch joins those contacts.
Look at a drawing with a cell and lamp and one loose lead. The lamp is off because the conducting path stops at the loose lead. Predict what changes when the model switch joins that gap.
A diagram lets us test a prediction by tracing the path. Start at either cell terminal. The path must pass through both lamp contacts and return to the other cell terminal.
Draw the symbol for the cell with two unequal marks. Keep their roles straight: the longer mark represents the positive terminal and the shorter mark is the negative terminal.
A circuit diagram records connections. A real lamp on the left can appear on the right in a simplified diagram if the same points stay connected.
Our lamp may be off even if the switch looks closed. A flat cell, damaged lamp or loose contact can all be possible reasons. In the kit, check one thing at a time with the teacher.

board.text: Check the cell, lamp and connections

text.en: A teacher’s test circuit has a small gap holding a sample. What happens when the sample is a metal paper clip? The clip can bridge that gap and let current pass.
Replace the clip with a dry plastic piece, using the same teacher-provided circuit. The lamp usually stays off because the plastic is a poor conductor of electric current.

board.text: Dry plastic is a poor conductor

text.en: When a lamp stays off, also check that the sample was touching both test contacts and that the kit works with a known metal sample. A poor connection can look like a non-conducting sample.

board.text: Check contact and compare with known metal

text.en: Put a wire on the board in cross-section. A metal centre provides a conducting path and the jacket is an insulating cover. The two materials do two different jobs.
Only use the small cells and parts provided for the classroom kit. Keep the kit away from wall sockets. Do not connect the two cell terminals directly to each other.

board.text: Include the intended device in the loop

text.en: The rest is a short circuit-pattern extension. In a series sketch there is one path. In a parallel sketch there are branches. Compare the diagrams by tracing where the paths split.

board.text: Extension: one path or branching paths

text.en: Before you finish, explain why the cell, lamp and wires are not enough by themselves. Trace one complete conducting path in a working setup and identify where an open switch breaks it.

board.text: Locate the break at the switch

problem.en: Why does the bulb not glow when the switch is open?

text.en: The switch makes a gap.
The loop is incomplete, so no current flows.

prompt.en: Explain how an open switch changes what happens in a torch circuit.

requiredIdeas.en: Opening the switch separates its contacts.
The conducting path through the lamp has a gap.

commonMisconceptions.en: A lamp will glow with only one of its two contacts connected.

points.en: A circuit needs a complete loop.
Conductors allow current; insulators do not.
Series: one path; parallel: many paths.
